hints: Think about what rate actually means in chemistry, how fast reactants are used up and how fast products form.
Statements 1 and 2 are the textbook definitions of rate, one tracks disappearance and the other tracks appearance.
Consider a gas syringe experiment at constant pressure, if the moles of gas change then volume change per time also tracks how fast the reaction is going.
walkthrough:
**Recall what reaction rate means**

Think of rate as change in amount per unit time. Reactants fall, products rise, so both changes tell you the speed.

Rate rule:
$$\text{rate} = -\frac{\Delta[\text{reactant}]}{\Delta t} = +\frac{\Delta[\text{product}]}{\Delta t}$$

**Check statements 1 and 2**

Statement 1 describes the decrease in reactant concentration per time. That is exactly the definition of rate.

Statement 2 describes the rate of appearance of a product. That is also exactly the definition of rate, just from the other side.

**Check statement 3 about volume**

At constant pressure, if a reaction produces or uses up gas, the total gas volume changes. Measuring that volume increase per second with a gas syringe is a standard practical method for rate.

Example idea:
$$\text{volume of gas collected per time} \propto \text{rate of reaction}$$

**Combine the conclusion**

Since 1, 2 and 3 can all be used to follow rate, the combination with all three is the correct choice.

options.A: Correct, because all three statements are valid ways to measure rate. 1 and 2 are the concentration definitions, and 3 is a practical gas volume method at constant pressure when moles of gas change.
options.B: Incorrect if this option includes only 1 and 2. It wrongly leaves out statement 3. Volume change at constant pressure is a well accepted way to follow a gas-evolving reaction, so it should be included.
options.C: Incorrect if this option omits statement 1. The decrease in reactant concentration per unit time is the fundamental definition of rate, so it cannot be left out.
options.D: Incorrect if this option includes only statement 1. It wrongly excludes the product-based definition and the volume method, both of which are equally valid for measuring rate.
